```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4.5,
  fig.align = "center"
)
library(distmer)
library(vegan)
library(ggplot2) 
library(kableExtra)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
```

A distance-based mixed model should be reproducible at three levels: the data
and ecological distance, the experimental design and permutation rule, and the
software result. `distmer` exposes each of these rather than treating a
pseudo-F and p-value as a black box.

This guide shows reference comparisons, deterministic package checks,
simulation tools, and a reporting record that can accompany a paper or data
release.

## Reference agreement on vegan data

For an independent one-factor design, the fixed-effect statistic has the same
dissimilarity-space definition as `vegan::adonis2()`. The following comparison
uses the `dune` communities and Bray--Curtis dissimilarity.

```{r adonis-reference}
data(dune, dune.env, package = "vegan")
dune_bray <- vegdist(dune, method = "bray")

distmer_fit <- permanova(
  dune_bray ~ Management, dune.env,
  permutations = 199, mc_permutations = 0, seed = 101
)
vegan_fit <- adonis2(
  dune_bray ~ Management, dune.env,
  permutations = 199
)

data.frame(
  implementation = c("distmer", "vegan::adonis2"),
  pseudo_f = c(distmer_fit$table$`Pseudo-F`[1], vegan_fit$F[1])
) |> 
  kbl(digits=3) |> 
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed")) 
```

The statistic should agree to numerical tolerance. Permutation p-values need
not be identical unless the two functions receive the identical permutation
matrix; recording only a seed does not guarantee that different packages draw
the same sequence of arrangements.

The dispersion companion can also be checked against
`vegan::betadisper()`.

```{r dispersion-reference}
selected <- dune.env$Management %in% c("NM", "SF")
two_group_distance <- vegdist(dune[selected, ], method = "bray")
two_group_env <- droplevels(dune.env[selected, , drop = FALSE])
dispersion_design <- compile_permanova_design(
  ~ Management, two_group_env, two_group_distance
)
distmer_dispersion <- permanova_dispersion(
  dispersion_design, term = "Management", type = "median",
  permutations = 199, seed = 101
)
vegan_dispersion <- betadisper(
  two_group_distance, two_group_env$Management, type = "median"
)

c(
  maximum_distance_difference = max(abs(
    distmer_dispersion$distances - vegan_dispersion$distances
  )),
  pseudo_f_difference = distmer_dispersion$test$statistic -
    unname(anova(vegan_dispersion)["Groups", "F value"])
) |> 
  kbl(digits=3) |> 
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed")) 
```

These are useful anchors, but validation is broader than agreement with one
package. Mixed designs are also checked against their univariate Euclidean
counterparts, exact enumeration, independent matrix calculations, and
operating-characteristic simulations.

## Run the deterministic checks

`run_permanova_validation()` performs the package's fast analytic battery. It
checks reference statistics, exact permutation counts, projector algebra,
retained non-Euclidean geometry, mixed-design denominators, and failure
boundaries.

```{r validation}
validation_report <- run_permanova_validation()
validation_report[, c("check", "passed", "metric")]
stopifnot(all(validation_report$passed))
```

Keep this report with the package version. A green report shows that the
installed code reproduces its pinned numeric checks on the current platform;
it does not certify that a new field design satisfies the package assumptions.

## Use simulations for a proposed design

Simulation asks a different question: how does a planned design behave under
known null, location-shift, and assumption-stress scenarios? The small run
below is intentionally only a code example so that the vignette builds quickly.

```{r simulation}
simulation <- simulate_mixed_validation(
  simulations = 5, permutations = 19,
  groups_per_treatment = 4, replicates = 3, seed = 101
)
simulation$summary[, c(
  "scenario", "estimand", "rejection_rate", "monte_carlo_se",
  "max_abs_denominator_f_difference"
)] |> 
  kbl(digits=3) |> 
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed")) 
```

```{r simulation-plot, fig.alt="Illustrative rejection rates from three mixed-model simulation scenarios"}
simulation_plot <- simulation$summary
ggplot(simulation_plot, aes(scenario, rejection_rate, fill = estimand)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(
      ymin = pmax(0, rejection_rate - 1.96 * monte_carlo_se),
      ymax = pmin(1, rejection_rate + 1.96 * monte_carlo_se)
    ),
    width = 0.15
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Five simulations are a smoke test, not calibration evidence",
       x = NULL, y = "Rejection proportion", fill = "Target") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 20, hjust = 1))
```

For scientific validation, increase the simulation count to hundreds or
thousands, use realistic abundance distributions and missingness, and report
binomial uncertainty. Include at least an exchangeable null, a plausible effect,
dispersion heterogeneity, heavy tails or outliers where relevant, and the exact
imbalance expected in the survey.

Specialised helpers cover nested, crossed, unbalanced, contrast, random-slope,
and strong-FWER designs. Their names are available with:

```{r helpers}
grep("^(simulate|audit)_.*validation$", getNamespaceExports("distmer"),
     value = TRUE)
```

## Make the fitted design auditable

A result contains more than its printed table. Preserve the elements that
identify the statistical question and exchangeability rule.

```{r audit-object}
names(distmer_fit)
distmer_fit$engine
distmer_fit$design$spectral[c(
  "euclidean", "negative_count", "negative_ratio", "correction"
)] |> 
  kbl(digits=3) |> 
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed")) 

distmer_fit$fit$tests$Management[c(
  "estimand", "exchangeable_units", "permutation_algorithm"
)] |> 
  kbl(digits=3) |> 
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed")) 

```

For mixed results, also retain the reported denominator, hierarchy assignment,
unit-centroid weighting, attainable permutation count, and any symmetry or
additivity assumption. `permanova_capabilities()` records the validated scope
and exclusions for every specialised implementation.

## A reproducible analysis pattern

```{r reproducible-template, eval=FALSE}
library(distmer)
library(vegan)

# 1. Freeze the input and ecological choices.
community <- read.csv("community.csv", row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE)
metadata <- read.csv("metadata.csv")
distance <- vegdist(community, method = "bray")

# 2. Fit with an explicit seed and enough permutations for the intended report.
fit <- permanova(
  distance ~ treatment + covariate + (1 | site),
  metadata, permutations = 9999, seed = 20260723
)

# 3. Save the complete result, not only a copied p-value.
saveRDS(
  list(
    fit = fit,
    distance_diagnostics = distance_diagnostics(distance),
    package_version = as.character(packageVersion("distmer")),
    session = sessionInfo()
  ),
  "distance-model-result.rds"
)
```

If the attainable permutation space is small, use `permutations = "all"` and
record that the result is exact. If Monte Carlo sampling is used, the minimum
possible p-value and its sampling variation should be compatible with the
claims being made.

## Reporting checklist

- data source, exclusions, transformations, and treatment of zeros;
- dissimilarity name and settings, plus signed-spectrum diagnostics;
- formula and Type I/II/III choice where applicable;
- experimental unit, nesting or crossing, denominator, and estimand;
- what moved in a permutation or sign flip, and within which strata;
- requested, attainable, and used permutation counts, plus the seed;
- location, dispersion, planned contrasts, and multiplicity method;
- `distmer`, `vegan`, and R versions and the saved fitted object;
- code and session information sufficient to reproduce every table and figure.

The package tests the algebra it claims to implement. The ecologist remains
responsible for showing that the distance, model, experimental unit, and
exchangeability assumptions represent the study that was actually conducted.
